articles.title: Child safety staff determined to send Elizabeth Struhs home with parents despite doctors’ concerns, inquest hears
articles.summary:
Queensland coronial inquest into death of eight-year-old girl continues after 14 members of religious sect were convicted of her manslaughter



It was impossible to change the mind…

blocks.text: It was impossible to change the mind of child safety staff after they had decided to send Elizabeth Struhs home with her parents despite some of her doctors’ concerns, a police officer has told a coronial inquest into the young girl’s death.

Child safety staff decided in 2019 that it would be “more detrimental” to not return Elizabeth, aged six at the time, to her Toowoomba home upon her discharge from hospital after suffering a coma due to diabetic ketoacidosis, a Queensland coroner heard.

Elizabeth died at home on 7 January 2022 after her parents withdrew the insulin she needed to survive type 1 diabetes. Her parents were members of a religious sect known as the Saints. The sect did not believe in medicine, and believed Elizabeth would be miraculously healed of her illness or raised from the dead, the inquest heard.
All 14 adult members of the sect were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including her father, Jason Struhs, and mother, Kerrie Struhs.

The coroner, Ainslie Kirkegaard, heard evidence on Monday from senior doctors at the Queensland children’s hospital who had repeatedly raised the alarm after Elizabeth was hospitalised in a 2019 incident.

Kerrie Struhs told the authorities at the time that she didn’t believe in medicine, and had discouraged Elizabeth’s father from seeking medical assistance and to instead trust in prayer, the coroner heard.
Both parents were convicted of not providing the necessaries of life to Elizabeth as a result of the incident, and Kerrie was jailed.

After Elizabeth was admitted to hospital in 2019, doctors warned that Kerrie might “sabotage” her long-term treatment for the incurable illness, which requires multiple insulin injections a day, if they lived together, the coroner heard.
But the court heard that child safety officers determined she should be returned home to the care of Jason.

The coroner heard evidence about a meeting held by the suspected child abuse and neglect team in which the decision was made. It was led by child safety officers, but involved specialist police and health staff.
Jason was deemed to be able to provide treatment for Elizabeth, such as insulin injections, the court heard.

According to minutes from the meeting, a child safety officer said: “The Queensland children’s hospital is not agreeing with our assessment and have been very vocal about it. I feel that removing her would be more detrimental and we currently have the father stepping up.”
On Tuesday, the court heard from a police officer who had attended the meeting. He told the court he’d served as a child safety liaison for 10 years.
“I learned early on … you couldn’t change child safety’s mind once they had made their decision,” the officer told the court.
“I was never going to change their mind regardless of what I said.”
The officer said the attitude was not confined to a single child safety officer.
after newsletter promotion
“It was across the board … they had their own structured decision making tools that they used and we had to respect their decision.”
The officer described the approach as “professional courtesy”.

Jason was initially willing to provide insulin to Elizabeth – against the wishes of his wife and their other children – but ceased doing so in 2021 after converting to his wife’s religious beliefs and joining her church group, leading to the child’s death.

A paediatrician specialist in child safety based at the Toowoomba hospital told the inquest on Tuesday that she was “generally happy” with the way child safety approached the case, including returning Elizabeth home.
According to notes taken at a meeting at the time and presented in court, the specialist said Elizabeth would be safe “as long as they are engaging with the hospital and diabetes educator”.
“If they stop showing up or engaging then it is likely we would put in a report as we would need to try and find out why.”
On Monday, two other doctors at the Queensland children’s hospital in Brisbane told the inquest that they were unhappy with the approach, which one labelled “entirely inadequate to address the risk”.

One told the coroner that there had been longstanding poor relations between the Brisbane and Toowoomba hospitals, and their advice was ignored. But the Toowoomba doctor denied the hospitals had a poor relationship.
No witnesses appearing at the inquest can be identified for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Ship sinks in new drone attack off Bulgaria, PM summons Russian ambassador
articles.summary: Bulgaria's prime minister says two merchant ships were hit by drones and he suspects Russia was behind the attacks.

blocks.text: A merchant ship has sunk after drones hit two vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.
He indicated Russia was suspected of the attacks and that he had called in its ambassador.

One of the ships went down 17 nautical miles (31km) east of Krapets and one crew member was saved, he said. The other, Ukrainian-owned vessel was hit by three drones 18 nautical miles from the town of Byala and all 15 crew were rescued, he added.

The drone attacks come a week after two other commercial ships were hit by sea and aerial drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. One of the ships, the Alfa Watan, sank and all 10 crew, including nine Syrians, are presumed dead.

Radev convened an emergency meeting on Tuesday and said he had summoned Russian envoy Eleonora Mitrofanova. Although there was no conclusive evidence of blame on "either side... the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation", he said.

Bulgaria is a Nato member and the prime minister said he would speak shortly to secretary general Mark Rutte. Radev had earlier asked Nato and the EU for technical assistance in investigating the 6 October attacks, indicating it was unclear whether Russia and Ukraine were behind them.
Radev came to office during the summer and has since rejected suggestions that he is "pro-Russian".

Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for the latest attacks and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke on Tuesday of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".
Russia's military has not publicly commented on the issue. It has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the Black Sea, particularly the western side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
The same day that two ships were targeted off Bulgaria last week, Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.
Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports - and cited attacks in the ports of Mykolaiv and Chornomorsk last week, along with one in the Black Sea.
However, Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.
Meeting with his security chiefs on Tuesday, Bulgaria's prime minister said: "Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable".

Radev identified one of the hit vessels as the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, which is registered in Ukraine's Odesa, saying that five its crew members were being treated for minor injuries. He gave no further details about the vessel that had sunk.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said "Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters... once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea.
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength," he added.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits
articles.summary: Germany long resisted tougher action against China because of retaliation fears. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin and Paris to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect…

image.caption: Germany and France are pushing for stronger EU trade defense tools amid rising Chinese competitionImage: DW

blocks.text: Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's unfair trade practices.
In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.

Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.
Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."
China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.
The cost of standing still

Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."
Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.
Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.

Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.
Why Berlin's China policy is changing

German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.

Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.

blocks.caption: VW, Audi and Porsche have announced workforce reductions totaling tens of thousands of jobs as the industry undergoes a huge transformationImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.

"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."
Industry pressure grows for trade defenses

Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:
"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.
According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.

While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.
Business groups question industrial policy proposals
The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, is meant to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.
Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.
How to dismantle China's stranglehold on raw materials?

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."

Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on the number of hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.
EU weights additional trade measures

Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half.
That could affect several millions vehicle exports from China to the EU over the next few years, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.

blocks.caption: Amid intense Chinese rivalry, the EU says it wants to restore industrial production in EuropeImage: Torsten Krüger/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.

MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion, versus $172 billion to the US.
This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.
"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

articles.title: Ex-president named leader of new DR Congo rebel coalition
articles.summary: Joseph Kabila had previously denied having links to the M23 rebels, which control much of eastern DR Congo.

blocks.text: Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has been named the leader of a new rebel coalition seeking to oust the government.

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it aimed to coordinate "resistance forces" to end "tyranny" in Democratic Republic of Congo and would pursue the goal "by all means, including force".

Its unveiling on Monday is the clearest indication so far of Kabila's direct involvement in an armed movement a year after he was sentenced to death in absentia for treason. He had previously denied having links to the M23 rebel group.
The Congolese government has not commented.
The coalition was announced at a press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma, the largest city in eastern DR Congo, which has been under the control of the M23 since last year.

M23 leader Sultani Makenga will serve as one of Kabila's four deputies in the new movement. The other three also come from the AFC-M23 alliance which last year seized much of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo.
The announcement of the new group comes days after Kabila delivered an address in which he said he would set out how Congolese people should act to "rescue" their country.
On Friday, Kabila accused President Félix Tshisekedi's government of disregarding proposals he had put forward last year, including some aimed at ending the conflict in eastern DR Congo.

Kabila also accused the government of undermining constitutional rule, mismanaging the economy and failing to improve security. He further alleged arbitrary arrests of political opponents and military officers.
The government has not publicly responded to those claims.
Kabila, 55, ruled DR Congo from 2001 until January 2019, when Tshisekedi took office following a disputed election.
The former president had remained largely out of public view for several years but has become increasingly critical of his successor's administration.
The formation of the new coalition comes at an uncertain time in a country that has been wracked by violence for decades.
More than 100 militia groups are active in eastern DR Congo amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources.
Tshisekedi's second term ends in 2028 but in May he said that elections, which are due then, may not be held because of the conflict.
He also hinted that he may seek re-election for a third term "if the people want".
The parliament has since passed a bill that could pave the way for a referendum that could remove the constitution's two-term limit.
Last month, authorities clashed with protesters holding demonstrations in the capital against the proposed changes.

articles.title: Two ships hit by drones of unknown origin off Bulgarian coast – Europe live
articles.summary:
Rescue operations underway after one vessel is sunk in the Black Sea and another damaged

Over in Warsaw, Poland’s parliament speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty is beginning his…

blocks.text: 11 crew members from sunken vessel hit by drone still missing near Bulgarian coast
The latest update from Bulgaria says that 11 crew members from the sunken ship are still missing.
The number of people rescued from the ship has now gone up to five, with authorities hoping they will be able to offer more insight into what happened overnight.
Key events

items: 4m ago'We are facing a really testing period' on Ukraine, Russian hybrid warfare, UK's Miliband says
8m agoSupport for Ukraine over the coming winter is critical, EU ministers say
15m ago11 crew members from sunken vessel hit by drone still missing near Bulgarian coast
32m agoMorning opening: Two ships hit by drones off Bulgarian coast

blocks.text: The ministers get asked about Trump’s diesel deal with Putin.
They don’t really offer any hot takes on this.
Germany’s Wadephul says that Europe needs to keep talking to Trump, and keep imposing sanctions on Russia.
Poland’s Sikorski makes a domestic point, putting pressure on Poland’s Maga-friendly president Karol Nawrocki to intervene with Trump directly.
Norway’s Espen Barth Eide also focuses on Europe’s resolve, more than anything else.
By the way, you can watch the Warsaw Security Forum panel with Barth Eide, Miliband, Sikorski, and Wadephul here.
'We are facing a really testing period' on Ukraine, Russian hybrid warfare, UK's Miliband says
UK’s Miliband is next.

He draws on his family’s history, saying his mother found refuge in Warsaw during the second world war, and he had “an amazing visit” to the Jewish Historical Institute this morning where he saw documents about his family’s history.
“It is a reminder of what war means for the ravaging of people’s lives and the uprooting of people’s lives.”
But he then moves on to Ukraine as he says:

“I think our job is not to be analysts, but to lead. We are four and a half years into this warm and the truth is that our resolve is being tested. Our resolve is being tested as far as Ukraine is concerned, resolve is being tested with Russian hybrid warfare, and our job is to stop and to respond. I feel a sense of confidence, but I don’t think we can be complacent at all. We are facing a really testing period. Putin is not winning this war, but him not winning is not good enough for us yet. And therefore what we do in the coming months, whether it is on sanctions, continuing to increase the pressure on Russia, whether it is the fiscal support for Ukraine, whether it’s defensive support for Ukraine, all of this really, really matters, and it matters morally, and it matters also to European security.”
Support for Ukraine over the coming winter is critical, EU ministers say
The four ministers are speaking now.
Poland’s Sikorski says he “regrets” that Europe “wasted” the first two years of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and is only now “catching up” when it comes to rearmaments.

“By the end of the decade, we will have a combined army, even just around the Baltic and the Eastern flank, that Putin would be crazy to attack. But if that is our calendar, that would be too late for Ukraine,” he says.
He says it’s critical to sustain Ukraine through the coming winter.
Germany’s Wadephul says Europe is “more united than we were at the beginning of the war,” and “have more capabilities.”
“The winter will be challenging, but we know what to do.”
Over in Warsaw, Poland’s parliament speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty is beginning his opening speech telling the audience that Europe is “at the turning point” of “civilisational” significance.
Addressing the Warsaw Security Forum, he says “for those who have any doubts that the president of the Russian Federation is a murderer and aggressor, and Ukraine is a victim.”
He says “it has to be said: there is no free Poland and free Europe, without a free Ukraine.”

Just as he says it, Poland issues a (now fairly routine) emergency alert to residents of a south-eastern region neighbouring Ukraine, putting them on high alert because of Russian strikes across the border.
The foreign ministers of Britain, Germany, Poland and Norway should be up on the main stage shortly.
Morning opening: Two ships hit by drones off Bulgarian coast

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Drones of unknown origin struck two ships in the Black Sea off Bulgaria this morning, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations, the country’s prime minister Rumen Radev said.

blocks.caption: Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev addresses the media following an incident in Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone last week. Photograph: Spasiyana Sergieva/Reuters

blocks.text: Only one person was rescued from the sunken vessel, and 15 people were picked up from the other one.
The attack comes exactly a week after a similar incident in which one ship sank with its crew on board, and the other one was evacuated, with 18 people rescued.
PM Radev said the attacks were “absolutely unacceptable,” and said he would seek assistance from Nato and the European Union.
He said that while there is no “clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility” yet, “the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.”
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said “the Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine.”

“This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea. We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable.”

The incident comes amid growing fears about Russia’s war against Ukraine and as several European foreign ministers meet at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, including Britain’s Ed Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul, and Ukraine’s Andrii Sybiha.
I will monitor their comments and bring you the top lines.
Separately, the French high school protests are expected to intensify today after key groups called for “a day of mobilisation” across the country.
Over in Spain, the Spanish royals are expected to visit the autonomous city of Ceuta in northern Africa, which continues to see its every day’s life disrupted by the migration crisis.

In Sweden, the Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson is due to report back on the progress of her talks on government formation today. But early reports suggest she does not quite have everything lined up yet, and the process is likely to take more time.

Finally, in the Vatican, Pope Leo is expected to be hospitalised today to remove a lung nodule discovered in his body to test it if the lesion is malignant. He is likely to stay there for about a week.
So, lots for us to cover. I will bring you all the key lines here.
It’s Monday, 13 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Andy Burnham will take Britain back into European Union, Neil Kinnock claims – UK politics live
articles.summary: Former Labour leader says he believes the prime minister has an ‘authentic commitment’ to taking the UK back into the EU

blocks.text: Good morning. In his long statement to MPs yesterday, Andy Burnham was evasive when asked whether he wanted his planned renegotiation of Britain’s relationship with the EU to result in a Labour-led government, after the next election, rejoining. In response to one question about this, Burnham told a Tory MP he was “getting way ahead of himself” with the question. But one well-placed observer is not being so coy.

Neil Kinnock, the former Labour leader and one of three people Burnham has named as his political mentors, has given an interview to la Repubblica, the Italian newspaper. He told it that he believes Burnham does want to, and will, take the UK back into the EU.
Kinnock said: “Andy makes the declaration of his determination to change the relationship, and it’s obvious that his objective is to join again.”
Asked again if he thought Burnham would be the person to take the UK back into the EU, Kinnock replied:

double quotation markYes, sure, sure, sure. His commitment is authentic. He really does understand from the grassroots up why restoring what I think of as normality in our continent is vital for every party economically, politically, culturally, all in security terms, and is able to articulate it in language that people can understand. So yeah, he is definitely.
Asked about Burnham playing down his desire to revisit the referendum result during the Makerfield byelection campaign, Kinnock claimed this was just a matter of deciding when to have this debate.

double quotation markAndy’s not changed direction. He’s always been a committed pro-European. In the byelection, he rightly didn’t make a noise about it. That’s tomorrow’s debate. Simply because the byelection wasn’t about Europe. It was about winning Makerfield in order to enable him to become leader of the party. That’s all it was about.

Kinnock was interviewed by Antonello Guerrera who asked how, as someone who inherited a leftwing party and dragged it to the right, Kinnock felt about a sucessor taking Labour to the left. Kinnock said he thought Burnham’s approach was right.

double quotation markIt’s common sense. It’s not left and right. Andy’s view of the engagement of the state is about what Winston Churchill did in the 1950s, and I don’t remember Churchill being thought of as on the left. Andy’s a socialist, but he’s a very common-sense socialist. He’s very rational. He’s cool, not just with his dark blue T-shirt, but in his thinking, and he’s advanced a hell of a lot in the last 10–12 years in terms of his understanding of the absolute importance of utility, of usefulness in politics. That’s what puts us, basically, he and I, on the same spot. Of course he’s on the left. I’m on the left. We’re socialists, but we are prompted by the usefulness of the application of ideas.

We have got a lobby briefing later and no doubt No 10 will clarify that its understanding of Burnham’s position on rejoining the EU is not quite the same as Kinnock’s. Kinnock is a former vice president of the European Commission, and an ardent pro-European, and perhaps there is some wishful thinking in what he says. But he is also a good friend of Burnham, and an astute observer of Labour politics. You will have to decide for yourself if he is right.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet.
Morning: Burnham attends meetings with business leaders in No 10.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: MPs debate the remaining stages of the courts and tribunals bill.
3pm: Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, gives evidence to the Commons defence committee.
5pm: Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, attends the regular weekly meeting of Lib Dem MPs, after two frontbenchers stood down amid concerns about his leadership.
Also today, another round of prisoner releases is happening under the prisoner early release scheme in England.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: 125 years of Thomas Mann's 'Buddenbrooks'
articles.summary: This over 1,000-page masterpiece offers a panoramic view of society in the 19th century and exposes the collapse of a merchant family: unrecognized sons, disillusioned daughters and the loss of…

image.caption: Thomas MannImage: picture-alliance/dpa

blocks.text: Who would have imagined it in the beginning? A 26-year-old man without a high school diploma, but greatly ambitious, writes a two-pound book with a melancholy undertone. "I'm not exactly delighted," his publisher initially responded. But he ended up publishing the novel anyway, more out of goodwill than conviction. And the rest is history.

For many, Thomas Mann's Buddenbrooks is considered THE German social novel. It is indeed a classic, and one that garnered the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. Global fame, an international best-seller, and required reading for many German students. Anyone who mentions Thomas Mann thinks of Buddenbrooks in the same breath. Why is that?
Life as a literary model
Does the explanation lie in the autobiographical connections between the work and the author?

Thomas Mann was born in Lübeck to a merchant family, but his artistic aspirations did not fit in well in the middle-class mainstream. This struggle inspired Mann's first work. The inability of this sensitive bohemian to carry on the family's time-honored business after the death of his father was sniffed at and derided.
'Buddenbrooks' by Thomas Mann

Reflecting the situation of his novel's character Hanno, Mann had a privileged life in a wealthy family, but one that was at risk of collapse. The aspiring novelist also had to withstand disappointing the expectations of others. He was forced to defend his dream of an artistic life. Yet as much as he was inspired by real life, he forcefully altered these biographical details to place his unique literary mark on his writing.
Appearance over substance

But does that really matter in light of people who choose not to make the distinction between an author's life and his work? Even though the name "Lübeck" does not appear in the novel, citizens there felt markedly insulted after the publication of Buddenbrooks in 1901.
That likely lies in the fact that the image the author portrayed was not one of an idyllic northern German city, but one of a place that had difficulty blending tradition with modernity.

blocks.caption: People were initially shocked over 'Buddenbrooks' in Lübeck, but now, Thomas Mann's statue stands tall in the cityImage: picture alliance/AP

blocks.text: This contradiction is also seen in each of the figures in the novel. Nothing is like it appears. Mann lays down this foundation of this skepticism from the very beginning, in a scene taking place on a very ordinary Thursday in October 1835. The Buddenbrook family comes together for their ordinary late lunch.

"There they all sat, on heavy, high-backed chairs, consuming good heavy food from good silver plates, drinking full-bodied wines and expressing their views freely on all subjects. When they began to talk shop, they slipped unconsciously more and more into dialect, and used the clumsy but comfortable idioms that seemed to embody to them the business efficiency and the easy well-being of their community. Sometimes they even used an over-drawn pronunciation by way of making fun of themselves and each other, and relished their clipped phrases and exaggerated vowels with the same heartiness they did their food."
Failing grandly

There sits the leader of the family company, Johann Buddenbrook the Elder, and his wife, his son and counsel Jean, along with his family. The grandchildren are also there: Tony the dreamer, the quarrelsome rebel Christian, and Thomas, the eldest grandchild.

It is Thomas who is supposed to later take on the responsibility of continuing the family tradition, regardless of the cost. Mann weaves his narrative work starting with this main family, and then across several generations.

But appearances in the family are deceptive. The reader senses it's all headed toward a downfall. The new house is taken over from a family that was once as illustrious as the Buddenbrooks, but faced financial ruin and had to leave.
Johann and his family aim to make a better go of it. They make decisions on what is demanded economically, but fail — financially, interpersonally, and mentally.

Tony and Thomas end up falling in love with people not befitting their social standing, but do not have the courage to stand up to their parents. They enter marriages of convenience, yet it is these partnerships that paradoxically set disaster in motion.
Language as a mirror

From an early age, Thomas Mann was influenced by Schopenhauer's pessimistic notion of the will being a blind force at work in the world. Thus, there is likewise no escape for the Buddenbrooks. They speak of emotions and morality, yet it is money and economics that steer the ship. Failure, decline and even death seem to be the only viable outcome.

Mann also punctuates this hopelessness in a stylistic manner, by consistently repeating entire passages word for word, or evoking motifs such as the family registry or the estate in all their various forms.

blocks.caption: Heinrich Breloer turned the novel into a film in 2008 Image: picture-alliance/dpa/Bavaria Film/S. Falke

blocks.text: The extent of this demise appears linguistically molded and exaggerated. The Buddenbrooks, this proud north German family of refinement, actually speaks the vernacular studded with empty French expressions. "Je, den Düwel ook, c'est la question, ma très chère demoiselle!"

The lowly servants, the courtesans, and the demi-monde: all of them speak the language of the street, raw and unpolished. In a virtuoso manner, Thomas Mann orchestrated this mass of voices into a panorama of society in the 19th century. The snobbishness on the part of the Buddenbrooks thus appears as a relic of a long lost time. It's a symbol of their inability to adapt to change and place their faith in progress.
Stuffy husbands and anxious sons

Yet the fact that this extensive work spanning several generations does not get weighed down by aesthetic excess is purely due to Mann's brilliance as an author. He is able to bring every one of his numerous characters to life in words. Life that is full of complexity, contradictions and ambiguities. Some of these characters accompany the reader page for page; others appear only briefly.

And yet one begins to contemplate how someone like Grünlich could become a dodgy, unscrupulous husband and catches oneself wanting to chase the fearful Hanno out of the music conservatory and yell to him: "Go, throw yourself into life! You are not a failure." It is precisely this empathy that spurs one on to read through the night and prompts one to chuckle at all the intricate sentences and philosophical digressions.
Thomas Mann: Buddenbrooks, Vintage Classics / Penguin Random House, (German title: Buddenbrooks, 1901). English translation: John E. Woods

Thomas Mann was born into a privileged Lübeck merchant family in 1875. He died in Zurich, Switzerland in 1955. "I am a townsman, a citizen, a child and a great-grandchild of German bourgeois society," the author once wrote about himself. Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 for his debut novel, Buddenbrooks. He also garnered numerous other prizes and honors for his extensive work, including Death in Venice (1911), The Magic Mountain (1924), and the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers (1933-1943). He emigrated to Switzerland in 1933, and to the US in 1938. From there, he made his famous radio commentaries in which he agitated against the Nazis. He returned to Switzerland in 1952.
This article was first published as part of the series 100 German must-reads.

articles.title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse resurrects the classic vampire hunting game in bold, bloody fashion
articles.summary: Belmont's Curse is mostly a roaring resurrection for the 40-year-old series — but its punishing difficulty could make it hard to recommend to newcomers to the genre.

image.caption: Rose Belmont is the new main character in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, the latest in the long-running Castlevania series of video games. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

blocks.text: Entertainment·Review
Belmont's Curse is mostly a roaring resurrection for the 40-year-old series — but its punishing difficulty could make it hard to recommend to newcomers to the genre.
It's an old-school adventure with flair, but Nintendo Switch version suffers from technical flaws
With its monster-fighting action, punishing difficulty and boppy soundtrack, 1986's Castlevania was a standout title on the Nintendo Entertainment System.

In the nearly 40 years since, the series has spawned dozens of sequels, spinoffs and crossover media. But the publisher, Japan's Konami, has let it slumber like a vampire in a coffin; its last new instalment came out in 2014.

Now, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse aims to bring in new and old fans alike by taking inspiration from the wildly different chapters of the series' history as well as independent games it's inspired over the years.

The result is mostly a roaring resurrection for the series blending old-school 2D exploration with breathtaking artistic direction — but its punishing difficulty could make it hard to recommend to newcomers to the genre.
Back to the Belmonts
Belmont's Curse puts players in control of Rose Belmont, monster hunter and daughter of Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades, two of the main characters from 1989's Castlevania 3: Dracula's Curse.
It's 1499 and Paris is burning, under attack from monsters of unknown origin. Trevor shuffles offscreen to look for the local bishop, while Rose looks for clues in the Paris streets.
Dracula's castle rises from the ground, surrounded by Paris in 1499. (All screenshots were captured from a build still in development.) (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

She's also inherited a curse — a blood-red mark creeping up her right arm — from her mother who succumbed to it after a battle with Dracula over 20 years prior. Losing control of her emotions and giving into hate risks turning Rose into a mindless monster not unlike her enemies.

Things quickly go from bad to worse. Only a few hours into the adventure, Trevor is captured and Dracula's castle rises from underneath Paris, seemingly destroying Notre Dame Cathedral in the process.

Various members of the Belmont family tree have been the main characters of most Castlevania games, and centring it back on them makes sense — not the least because Trevor and Sypha recently starred in the Netflix Castlevania animated series. Through the game's roughly 15- to 20-hour runtime, however, the story will plumb both obvious and surprising corners of the series' decades-long history.
Dynamic combat and movement

Belmont's Curse roughly follows the same format as the fan-favourite 1997 entry Symphony of the Night. Taking cues from Nintendo's Metroid and Zelda series, Rose can explore Paris and Dracula's castle with its labyrinthine and interlocking locations, from an eerie cemetery where ghosts haunt visitors freely, or a clock tower full of giant metal gears and deadly machinery.
Rather than completing linear levels in sequence, players will run into dead ends or impassable hazards, eventually returning to them after discovering a new ability or equipment.
Dangerous traps and obstacles litter Paris and Dracula's castle. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

Early on, for example, Rose gets a whip that she can use to swing over spike traps or lasso enemies, opening them up for an exhilarating powerful attack with her weapons including swords, lances and yes, more whips.

The so-called "Metroidvania" formula is a proven one, and it feels like coming back home seeing it here after years of indie games imitating and iterating upon it — such as the mega-popular Hollow Knight: Silksong from last year.
Rose uses a whip made of magical light as a grappling hook. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)
It's hard. Maybe too hard?

Players should use caution, however — while familiar monster types rear their heads again such as zombies, skeletons and floating medusa heads, everyone moves faster and hits much harder than in past entries.

You'll have to use all your wits and reflexes to get Rose through some pitched battles, especially early on as her health and magic resources start small unless she finds upgrades hidden throughout the map.
Rose battles Medusa in an early boss fight. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

Even more punishing are the trap rooms — spinning razor blades, spiky pits and more arranged in devilish gauntlets that require timing just a little too precise, or jumping through gaps just a little too narrow to do reliably. Every new ability you find that theoretically makes them easier to navigate, only allows the level designers to add new ways to torment you.
Retracing your steps

This can make the need to backtrack and explore previously-seen areas all the more grating. Most older Castlevania games in this mold were fairly generous with rooms where you can save your progress and heal up, or warp rooms to zip back to relative safety.

Such sanctuaries are relatively rare in Belmont's Curse. Too often you'll need to backtrack for minutes at a time before reaching anything new, or even a place to breathe before planning your next route.
A section of the map in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, showing the interconnected parts of Paris the player must explore. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)
There are difficulty settings that, for example, let you adjust how much damage enemies' strikes inflict on Rose; but they don't ease the trap rooms' demands or make backtracking less tiresome.
Striking art and soundtrack
Despite the occasional frustrations navigating the maze that is Belmont's Curse, the package is elevated by exceptional presentation and art direction.

Paris is swathed in brilliant colour palettes from the pitch-black catacombs with flickering orange or eerie green flames puncturing the darkness; to the relatively serene cemetery's verdant greens and yellows getting gradually more poisonous as you delve deeper into its dangerous sewers.
Players can find items to upgrade their health and magic levels in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

Perhaps the height of it is the first approach to Dracula's castle, an impossibly huge and baroque structure set atop the ruins of Paris, supporting chain links the size of buildings anchoring it to the ground, as Rose whips and slashes her way through stone gargoyles haunted suits of armour — all set to a booming remix of the series classic song Bloody Tears.

Special mention goes to the soundtrack in general, a mostly brand-new group of tracks effortlessly mixing the series' usual classical foundation of choral chants and organ pipes with lo-fi beats and even the occasional dubstep reverberations.
A giant skull looms over Rose in the catacombs below Paris. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)
The story is also anchored by surprisingly poignant performances by voice actors, particularly Abby Trott as Rose and JB Blanc as a remorseful creature initially known only as The Fallen.
Switch version seriously falters

A word of caution, however: the Nintendo Switch version suffered from serious performance flaws in the review period as it was released on the original hardware and not the newer Switch 2 (though it can be played on either).

We experienced grainy, low-res visuals and longer load times on that platform, but worst was significant input delay between pressing a button and Rose moving or jumping on the screen. In a game that requires near-instant reaction times, this made the experience nearly unplayable.

The visuals and responsiveness were much better on the Xbox Series X version we played to completion. Konami says a Day 1 update will improve these issues on all platforms, but it wasn't available by the time this review was filed.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jonathan Ore is a writer and editor for CBC Radio Digital in Toronto. He regularly covers the video games industry for CBC Radio programs across the country and has also covered arts & entertainment, technology and the games industry for CBC News. You can reach him at jonathan.ore@cbc.ca

articles.title: Pope Leo in Rome hospital for lung surgery
articles.summary: Leo has been unusually candid for a pontiff about his health issues, disclosing the surgery to thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.

image.caption: The surgery marks the first major health issue of Leo's 17-month papacyImage: Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV is to undergo surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung, the Vatican has confirmed, and determine if it is cancerous.
He is being seen at Rome's prestigious Gemelli hospital, which has been the main site of treatment for popes for decades.
Shift in transparency
Leo, 71, disclosed the issue to thousands of worshippers at a prayer service on Sunday, making a marked shift in the level of transparency about his health compared to his predecessors.
In the past, the Vatican has often been accused of making confusing or extremely vague statements about popes' health, if revealing at information at all.
Pope Leo to undergo lung nodule surgery

The pontiff will be put under general anesthesia and require a weeklong hospital stay. All of his engagements have been cancelled through October 20. He is still likely to take a planned trip to South America in November.
According to oncologists, this type of surgery is usually necessary to determine if a lump is malignant. However, if it is, Leo has an excellent prognosis since it was caught so early.

articles.title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
articles.summary:
Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift

A…

blocks.text: A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.

The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.

The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.

The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.

blocks.caption: Spanish customs officials in Vigo, Galicia, unload bundles of cocaine from a sailing boat that was seized with more than 2,000kg of the drug last month.   Photograph: Salvador Sas/EPA

blocks.text: These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.

Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.

“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”

Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.

The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, a Europol report in 2103 warned of their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.

blocks.caption: Drug traffickers near Boa Vista, in Brazil’s northern state of Roraima, in 2024. The First Capital Command (PCC) is South America’s largest criminal group.  Photograph: Washington Post/Getty

blocks.text: A Europol report this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”
Interpol, led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.

The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reach a record of about 4,100 tonnes in 2024. This comes after growth of up to 35% at the beginning of the decade. More cocaine is now produced in Colombia than during the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar. Nearly all the world’s cocaine and many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.

Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”

He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”

blocks.caption: Soldiers and police raid a house seized by drug traffickers in Duran, Ecuador, in 2024. The country has become a key trafficking route for drugs.   Photograph: Gerardo Menoscal/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report on illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.

Europe has emerged as a key market because it offers organisations higher profit margins than the US. Since the beginning of the decade, European police have confiscated more drugs than American forces, and data indicates that Europe now represents about a quarter of global consumption.

Europol recently reported that out of 731 MTCNs operating across Europe, 149 are connected to Latin American organisations. Of these, 67 have Latin American members, and 22 mainly consist of Latin Americans.

articles.title: Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage
articles.summary: Marches in Delhi against changes to voting registration led to dragnets, internet blackouts – and questions about India’s electoral independence. Plus, the cinematographer capturing the beauty of…

blocks.text: Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.

Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.

The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.

“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.

The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.

While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.

blocks.caption: An activist tries to stop a police bus carrying detained protesters during a demo seeking the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner. Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/Reuters

blocks.text: The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.

The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.

Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.

Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.

As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”

On Monday, the Kerelam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: South African jurist and former UN human rights chief Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel peace prize. Photograph: Daniel Karmann/DPA/AP

blocks.text: Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.

Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.

Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. Photograph: Mayank Austen Soofi

blocks.text: With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Koushila Markam holds a photo of her daughter, Bamita Markam, who died from measles during an outbreak in Balaghat. Photograph: BBC News

blocks.text: At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: A quiet moment between Arbab Kamal Khan’s parents, whose everyday intimacy features in his photographs.

blocks.text: For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”

For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

articles.title: What is holding back Cyprus's Schengen ambitions?
articles.summary: The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area. Yet questions relating to the island's division and British military bases could still complicate its path to Europe's…

image.caption: There are nine designated crossing points between the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island. Pictured here: the Leda Street crossing point in NicosiaImage: Mpalis/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.
Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.
After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.

The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.

On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."

blocks.caption: Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration, Nicholas Ioannides, says Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, Europe's border-free travel zone, which covers 29 EU and non-EU countriesImage: Markus Lenhardt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.
Austria, the Netherlands express reservations
However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.
Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.

According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.
Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.
Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.
What is the Green Line?
Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.

blocks.caption: The buffer zone between the two parts of the island is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP)Image: STR/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.
The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.
Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.

This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.

"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.

"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.
Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?

Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.
Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.

The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.
Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.

Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."

"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.

According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.
Political negotiations with EU countries
In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.

Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.

blocks.caption: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was in Cyprus this summer in what was seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process on the islandImage: Ali Ruhluel/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.
In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.
Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.

The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.
